title: AF after ischemic stroke: anticoagulation timing
summary: Early oral anticoagulation is reasonable and low risk versus a delayed start in carefully selected (e.g., milder) AF-associated ischemic stroke (AHA 2026, 2a), although its efficacy against early recurrence is not established. CATALYST (5,441 patients from 4 trials; published after the AHA 2026 evidence-review cutoff): starting within 4 days vs day 5 or later reduced 30-day recurrent ischemic stroke, sICH or unclassified stroke (2.1 vs 3.0%; OR 0.70), with identical sICH (0.4%). ELAN schedule: within 48 h for minor or moderate and day 6–7 for major imaging-defined infarcts. OPTIMAS: within 4 days was noninferior to days 7–14 (3.3% each).

recommendations.text: In carefully selected (e.g., milder severity) AIS patients with atrial fibrillation, a strategy of early oral anticoagulation post-stroke is low risk and is reasonable compared with delayed anticoagulation, although the efficacy of early anticoagulation for preventing early recurrent stroke is not established.

In stroke or TIA patients with AF who do not have moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis or a mechanical heart valve, a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban, or rivaroxaban) is recommended over warfarin to reduce recurrent stroke risk.

consider: Size the infarct on imaging (ELAN categories), not by NIHSS alone; brain imaging before starting may be considered (AHA 2021, 2b).

ELAN infarct size: minor ≤1.5 cm; moderate involves a cortical superficial branch of the MCA, ACA or PCA, a deep MCA branch or the internal border zone; major involves an entire MCA, ACA or PCA territory, two or more MCA cortical branches, cortical plus deep MCA branches, or a brainstem or cerebellar lesion >1.5 cm (ELAN, NEJM 2023).
Hemorrhagic transformation: starting or continuing anticoagulation may be considered case by case (AHA 2026, 2b).
TIA with nonvalvular AF: starting anticoagulation immediately is reasonable (AHA 2021, 2a, expert opinion).
caution: Trial schedules guide but do not set an individual start date for very large infarcts or significant hemorrhagic transformation.

title: Stroke mechanism, ESUS and rhythm monitoring
summary: Complete or start the etiologic workup within 48 h of onset to guide prevention: brain CT or MRI, ECG, and CBC, coagulation, glucose, HbA1c, creatinine and lipids (AHA 2021, COR 1), plus carotid imaging for revascularization candidates (COR 1) and intracranial and vertebrobasilar imaging (2a). Cryptogenic stroke: echocardiography and prolonged rhythm monitoring are reasonable (2a) — CRYSTAL AF found AF in 12.4 vs 2.0% at 12 months with an implantable monitor. ESUS: antiplatelet, not empiric anticoagulation — NAVIGATE ESUS (rivaroxaban), RE-SPECT ESUS (dabigatran) and ARCADIA (apixaban for atrial cardiopathy) were neutral.
consider: Classify the mechanism (TOAST); an incomplete workup leaves it undetermined and does not establish ESUS.
ESUS: TEE, cardiac CT or cardiac MRI might be reasonable to find cardioaortic sources (2b).
Who reviews the monitor and acts on AF?
caution: A brief negative ECG does not exclude paroxysmal AF.

title: TOAST classification and stroke mechanism
summary: TOAST sorts ischemic stroke into five subtypes (large-artery atherosclerosis, cardioembolism, small-vessel occlusion, other determined etiology and undetermined etiology), with possible or probable diagnoses by the clinician's certainty; in its original test two neurologists agreed in 19 of 20 patients. Assign the subtype after brain imaging, vessel imaging and cardiac evaluation, because the mechanism decides prevention (antiplatelet or anticoagulant, revascularization, PFO closure).
consider: An incomplete workup leaves the mechanism undetermined; it does not establish ESUS.
DWI pattern helps: a single deep lacune suggests small-vessel disease, scattered emboli in several territories a cardiac source, and a watershed pattern large-artery disease (AHA TIA statement).

Pure lateral medullary infarction (n=130; angiography in 123): vertebral artery disease in 67% and PICA disease in 10%; presumed mechanisms included large-vessel 50%, dissection 15%, small-vessel 13% and cardioembolic 5%.
caution: TOAST was built to classify trial participants; it does not replace an individual mechanism review.

title: PFO: attribution and closure discussion
summary: PFO closure with long-term antiplatelet therapy is reasonable for ages 18–60 with nonlacunar stroke of undetermined cause after a full evaluation and a PFO with high-risk anatomic features (AHA 2021, 2a); without them AHA rates the benefit uncertain (2b), but ESO 2024 recommends closure when PASCAL rates the PFO possibly or probably causal. RESPECT: recurrent ischemic stroke 0.58 vs 1.07 per 100 patient-years (HR 0.55) over a median 5.9 years; CLOSE: 0/238 vs 14/235 strokes over a mean 5.3 years. Closure adds AF (CLOSE 4.6 vs 0.9%) and venous thromboembolism (RESPECT).
consider: Exclude competing causes first: vessel imaging, prolonged rhythm monitoring and echocardiography with a bubble study.

Use RoPE and PASCAL to judge causality: in pooled trial data (SCOPE), closure reduced stroke when PASCAL rated the PFO possible or probable (HR 0.38 and 0.10) but not unlikely (HR 1.14); AF beyond day 45 rose with closure in unlikely (+4.4%) and possible (+1.5%) categories.

Discuss procedural risk, AF and the long-term antiplatelet plan with the closure team. ESO 2024 suggests closure plus antiplatelet therapy over long-term anticoagulation alone (possible or probable PASCAL; low certainty); if closure is declined, individualize antiplatelet versus anticoagulant therapy (expert consensus).
caution: Evidence over age 60 and for an incidental PFO is limited.

title: Carotid stenosis: symptoms, severity and referral
summary: TIA or nondisabling stroke within 6 months with ipsilateral 70–99% stenosis: endarterectomy if perioperative stroke or death risk is <6% (AHA 2021, COR 1), ideally within 2 weeks (2a); 50–69%: endarterectomy depending on patient factors (COR 1); <50%: no revascularization (COR 3: No Benefit). At age ≥70 or within the first week, endarterectomy is preferred over stenting (2a). Asymptomatic: for >70% stenosis, AHA 2024 recommends shared decision-making on revascularization versus medical management (COR 1); at low perioperative risk, adding revascularization to intensive medical therapy may be reasonable (2b). ESO 2021 recommends endarterectomy for 60–99% stenosis at increased stroke risk on best medical therapy (moderate-quality evidence). Postdating both, CREST-2 (≥70%) found fewer 4-year events with stenting plus intensive medical management (2.8 vs 6.0%) but no significant benefit from endarterectomy (3.7 vs 5.3%); ACST-2 (2021) found stenting and endarterectomy similar (5-year non-procedural stroke 5.3 vs 4.5%).

recommendations.text: CEA is recommended for patients with TIA or nondisabling ischemic stroke within the past 6 months and ipsilateral severe (70-99%) carotid stenosis to reduce future stroke risk, provided the estimated perioperative morbidity and mortality is below 6%.

When carotid revascularization is indicated for TIA or nondisabling stroke, it is reasonable to perform the procedure within 2 weeks of the index event rather than delaying surgery, to increase the likelihood of a stroke-free outcome.

consider: How was the stenosis measured (NASCET), and does the lesion explain the event?
Large or disabling infarct, hemorrhage or near-occlusion: individualize timing with vascular surgery.
Everyone gets intensive medical therapy: antiplatelet, statin and BP control (COR 1).
caution: CREST-2 ran two separate trials, so it does not compare stenting directly with endarterectomy.

title: Symptomatic intracranial atherosclerosis
summary: Severe (70–99%) intracranial stenosis with stroke or TIA within 30 days: aspirin plus clopidogrel for up to 90 days (AHA 2021, 2a; AAN 2022, when hemorrhagic-transformation risk is low), plus high-intensity statin with LDL <70 mg/dL, long-term SBP <140 and exercise (COR 1). No angioplasty or stenting as first treatment (COR 3: Harm) — SAMMPRIS: 30-day stroke or death 14.7 vs 5.8% with stenting. BASIS (China, 2024; after AHA 2021 and AAN 2022): at ages 35–80 with TIA within 90 days or stroke 14–90 days earlier, submaximal balloon angioplasty plus medical therapy lowered a 1-year composite that included later revascularization of the qualifying artery (4.4 vs 13.5%), but 30-day stroke or death was 3.2 vs 1.6% and dissection occurred in 14.5%. AAN 2022 advises against routine angioplasty alone outside trials, and ESO 2022 against first-line angioplasty or stenting.
consider: Confirm the stenosis is symptomatic and in the right territory; 50–69% stenosis gets medical therapy (stenting is harmful).
Write the DAPT stop date and the single agent to continue.
Recurrent events despite therapy: recheck adherence and mechanism; the usefulness of angioplasty or stenting is unknown (2b).
caution: Long-term BP targets do not apply in the acute, perfusion-dependent phase.

title: Cervical artery dissection
summary: Extracranial carotid or vertebral dissection with stroke or TIA: give antithrombotic therapy for at least 3 months (AHA 2021, COR 1) — antiplatelet or anticoagulant are both reasonable (AHA 2026, 2a), but a large infarct, hemorrhagic transformation or intradural extension may favor antiplatelet therapy (AHA 2024). CADISS found no difference (stroke or death 3/126 vs 1/124); TREAT-CAD did not show aspirin noninferior to a vitamin K antagonist (composite 23 vs 15%; 7 ischemic strokes vs none). Pooled CADISS/TREAT-CAD participant data (444 patients): 90-day ischemic stroke, death or major bleeding 1.4% with anticoagulation vs 4.4% with antiplatelets (P=0.06, not significant), with fewer strokes (OR 0.14) but 2 vs 0 bleeding events. AHA 2024 suggests individualizing the choice for at least 3–6 months.

recommendations.text: In AIS patients with extracranial carotid or vertebral arterial dissection, treatment with either antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for at least 3 months is reasonable to prevent recurrent stroke.

consider: Confirm on CTA or MRI/MRA and separate cervical from intracranial or aortic dissection.
Recurrent events despite antithrombotics: endovascular therapy may be considered (AHA 2021, 2b).
Look for an underlying arteriopathy such as FMD when the history suggests it.
caution: Neither trial was powered to prove equivalence, and DOACs were not tested.

title: Secondary prevention and medication review
summary: Noncardioembolic stroke or TIA: antiplatelet rather than anticoagulant (COR 1); DAPT only short term (minor stroke [NIHSS ≤3] or high-risk TIA [ABCD2 ≥4] without IVT, started within 24 h: 21 days, AHA 2026 COR 1; severe intracranial stenosis: up to 90 days). BP <130/80 for most (AHA 2021, COR 1). Atherosclerotic stroke: statin ± ezetimibe to LDL <70 mg/dL (COR 1); no known coronary disease or major cardiac source and LDL >100: atorvastatin 80 mg (SPARCL). Diabetes: glucose-lowering drugs with proven cardiovascular benefit (AHA 2021, COR 1). Recheck lipids 4–12 weeks after a change, then every 3–12 months.

recommendations.text: Antiplatelet therapy is recommended over oral anticoagulation for patients with noncardioembolic ischemic stroke or TIA to reduce recurrent ischemic stroke and other cardiovascular events while minimizing bleeding risk.
An office BP goal of less than 130/80 mmHg is recommended for most hypertensive stroke or TIA patients to reduce recurrent stroke and vascular events.

For ischemic stroke or TIA patients with atherosclerotic disease (intracranial, carotid, aortic, or coronary), lipid-lowering therapy with a statin (plus ezetimibe if needed) to achieve an LDL-C goal below 70 mg/dL is recommended to reduce major cardiovascular events.

consider: Is the mechanism settled, and does it change the drug (AF, PFO, dissection, intracranial stenosis)?
Very high risk (stroke plus another major ASCVD event, or ≥2 high-risk conditions): ACC/AHA 2026 goal LDL-C <55 mg/dL; add ezetimibe and/or a PCSK9 antibody as needed (COR 1).
Check adherence, cost, smoking, diet and activity at every visit.
caution: Avoid indefinite DAPT or antiplatelet-plus-anticoagulant combinations without a separate indication.

title: Recovery, rehabilitation and follow-up
summary: AHA/ASA AIS 2026: formal inpatient interdisciplinary assessment and rehabilitation matched to the patient (COR 1); no high-dose, very early mobilization within 24 h of stroke onset (COR 3: Harm); screen for depression with a structured inventory and treat diagnosed depression (COR 1). SSRIs are not recommended for motor or functional recovery (COR 3: No Benefit): fluoxetine 20 mg daily for 6 months did not improve mRS and increased fractures (FOCUS, AFFINITY, EFFECTS), when started 2–15 days after stroke; this does not apply to treating diagnosed depression. Reassess function, mood and goals at follow-up.
consider: Which impairments, daily activities and participation goals need assessment or renewed therapy?
Have the patient and care partner received education, training and support?
Is follow-up feasible (transport, access, telehealth), and who reassesses progress?
caution: A screening score is not a diagnosis, and this card gives no driving, work or travel clearance. Grades are from AHA/ASA AIS 2026 (acute ischemic stroke); the August 2026 AHA/ASA rehabilitation guideline was not reviewed.
